parts.problem_md:
To help reduce the amount of traffic in a city, the mayor of the city has implemented a new daily driving charge on the ring road, which will last for a year.

The mayor is also interested in the amount of carbon dioxide emitted by road traffic.

An average vehicle is known to emit around 0.1 kg/km of carbon dioxide.

If the radius of the circular ring road is 8 km, show that an average vehicle would emit around 5.03 kilograms of carbon dioxide when doing one full lap of the ring road.
parts.solution_md:
> *Find the length of one full lap of the ring road by finding the circumference of the ring road*

> *The circumference of a circle is found using the formula *$C=2πr$*, for a radius *$r$

> *Substitute *$r=8$* into the formula*

$C=2\timesπ\times8$

**[1]**

> *Find the length of the ring road*

$16π=50.265482...\mathrm{km}$

> *An average vehicle emits 0.1 kg of carbon dioxide for every 1 km travelled*

> *Find the carbon dioxide emission of one lap by multiplying the road length by 0.1*

** **$16 \mathrm{\pi } \times 0.1 = 5.02654 = 5.03 \text{kg} ( 3 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} )$**[1]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

An average vehicle is known to emit around 0.1 kg/km of carbon dioxide. If the radius of the circular ring road is 8 km, show that an average vehicle would emit around 5.03 kilograms of carbon dioxide when doing one full lap of the ring road.

The mayor assumes that an average vehicle travels** half **a lap of the ring road every day.

The variable $c$ is the total amount of carbon dioxide emitted by** all **vehicles on the ring road per day, measured in kilograms.

Find the value of $k$ in the relationship

$c=kN$

where $N$ is the number of vehicles per day, measured in tens of thousands.

Give your value of $k$ correct to 2 significant figures.
parts.solution_md:
> *Find the assumed carbon emitted per day per vehicle, *$d$* kg, by dividing your answer from (a) by 2*

$d=\frac{5.03}{2}\mathrm{kg}$

> $N$* is measured in tens of thousands per day, so *$10000N$* is the total number of vehicles per day*

> *Find the assumed carbon dioxide emitted per day by *$10000N$* vehicles, by multiplying *$d$* by *$10000N$

$\begin{gathered} c = \frac{5.03}{2} \times 10 000 N \text{kg} \\ = 25150 N \text{kg} \end{gathered}$

**Either half answer from (a) or multiplying by **$10000N$**seen [1]**

> *Round the answer to 2 significant figures*

** **$k = 25000 ( 2 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$ **[1]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The mayor assumes that an average vehicle travels half a lap of the ring road every day. The variable c is the total amount of carbon dioxide emitted by all vehicles on the ring road per day, measured in kilograms. Find the value of k in the relationship c = kN where N is the number of vehicles per day, measured in tens of thousands. Give your value of k correct to 2 significant figures.

A cubic model used to calculate the traffic on the ring road is given by

$N = \frac{1}{108} ( t^{3} - 21 t^{2} + 72 t + 540 )$

where $N$ is the number of vehicles per day, measured in tens of thousands, and $t$ is the time, measured in months, from the date of the driving charge being introduced.

The mayor wants to adapt the cubic model into a model that shows:

- the total amount of carbon dioxide emitted by** **all vehicles on the ring road per day, $c$, measured in kilograms
- against the time, $t$, measured in months, from the date of the driving charge being introduced

Use the information in part (b) to write down a cubic model for $c$ in terms of $t$.
parts.solution_md:
> *Start with the cubic model *$N = \frac{1}{108} ( t^{3} - 21 t^{2} + 72 t + 540 )$

> *Substitute this into the model for *$c$* in terms of *$N$* found in part (b)*

$\begin{gathered} c = 25000 N \\ = 25000 ( \frac{1}{108} ( t^{3} - 21 t^{2} + 72 t + 540 ) ) \end{gathered}$

> *This form is a correct answer, but can be simplified*

$\begin{gathered} c = \frac{25000}{108} ( t^{3} - 21 t^{2} + 72 t + 540 ) \end{gathered}$

$c = \frac{6250}{27} ( t^{3} - 21 t^{2} + 72 t + 540 )$** [1]**

To help reduce the amount of traffic in a city, the mayor of the city has implemented a new daily driving charge on the ring road, which will last for a year.

The scatter graph below shows the number of vehicles per day, $N$, measured in tens of thousands, that use the ring road against the time, $t$, measured in months, from the date of the driving charge being introduced.

![Scatter graph showing a decline in daily vehicle numbers over 12 months after a driving charge was introduced.](assets/001-scatter-graph-showing-a-decline-in-daily-vehicle.png)

The mayor suspects that the reduction in traffic will eventually settle to a positive value, rather than decrease to zero.

A cubic model is proposed.

A data analyst inputs the data from the scatter graph into a computer to find the closest matching cubic curve.

The computer outputs:

$N = \frac{1}{108} ( t^{3} - 21 t^{2} + 72 t + 540 )$

Sketch this model on the axes provided.

parts.problem_md:
To help reduce the amount of traffic in a city, the mayor of the city has implemented a new daily driving charge on the ring road, which will last for a year.

The scatter graph below shows the number of vehicles per day, $N$, measured in tens of thousands, that use the ring road against the time, $t$, measured in months, from the date of the driving charge being introduced.

![Scatter graph showing a decline in daily vehicle numbers over 12 months after a driving charge was introduced.](assets/001-scatter-graph-showing-a-decline-in-daily-vehicle.png)

The mayor notices that there is a slight increase in road traffic immediately after the driving charge is introduced, after which the traffic starts to decrease.

The mayor believes this is due to a delay in drivers realising that the new charge had been introduced.

To model this delay, a negative quadratic model is proposed in the form

$N = - \frac{1}{12} ( t + 6 ) ( t - 10 )$

A sketch of this model is shown below.

![Scatter graph showing vehicle numbers decreasing over 12 months after a charge introduction, with a quadratic curve fitted to the data.](assets/004-scatter-graph-showing-vehicle-numbers-decreasing.png)

Find the values of the axes intercepts, $p$ and $q$.
parts.solution_md:
> *Method 1: Using GDC*

> *Open the graphing software on your calculator and plot the graph of *$\mathrm{f} ( x ) = - \frac{1}{12} ( x + 6 ) ( x - 10 )$

> *Navigate to the points of intersection of the graph with the axes (you can ignore the negative *$x$*-intercept)*

> *The *$y$*-intercept is *$( 0 , 5 )$

$p=5$ **[1]**

> *The positive *$x$*-intercept is *$( 10 , 0 )$

$q=10$ **[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *The equation is given in factorised form, so each factor can be used to find a zero of the graph*

> *Setting the first factor to zero and solving gives:*

$\begin{gathered} ( t + 6 ) & = 0 \\ t = - 6 \end{gathered}$

> *Setting the second factor to zero and solving gives:*

$\begin{gathered} ( t - 10 ) & = 0 \\ t = 10 \end{gathered}$

> *The negative *$x$*-intercept can be ignored*

$q=10$ **[1]**

> *The *$y$*-intercept will be the constant term of the expanded equation*

> *This can be found by multiplying the two constant terms with *$-\frac{1}{12}$* (or by substituting in *$t=0$*)*

$-\frac{1}{12}\times6\times-10=-\frac{1}{12}\times-60$

$p=5$ **[1]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

N = -1/12 (t + 6)(t - 10)

The maximum point on the model occurs 2 months after the driving charge is introduced.

Find the maximum number of vehicles per day predicted by this model.

Give your answer correct to the nearest hundred.
parts.solution_md:
> *Method 1: Using GDC*

> *Open the graphing software on your calculator and plot the graph of *$\mathrm{f} ( x ) = - \frac{1}{12} ( x + 6 ) ( x - 10 )$

> *Navigate to the maximum point on the graph (at the turning point)*

> *The *$x$*-coordinate should be 2, the *$y$*-coordinate gives the value you need*

$( 2 , \frac{16}{3} )$

**[1]**

> *Remember that the value of *$N$* is measured in tens of thousands, so multiply your answer by *$10000$

$\frac{16}{3}\times10000=53333.333....$

> *Round your answer to the nearest hundred*

** 53 300** **[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *Two months after the ring road was introduced will be at the point when *$t=2$

> *Substitute *$t=2$* into the equation of the negative quadratic model*

$N = - \frac{1}{12} ( 2 + 6 ) ( 2 - 10 )$

**[1]**

> *Use your calculator to find the answer*

$N=-\frac{1}{12}\times8\times-8=\frac{16}{3}$

> *Remember that the value of *$N$* is measured in tens of thousands, so multiply your answer by *$10000$

$\frac{16}{3}\times10000=53333.333....$

> *Round your answer to the nearest hundred*

** 53 300** **[1]**

parts.problem_md:
This task looks at models for daily road traffic on a circular ring road around a city.

To help reduce the amount of traffic, the mayor of the city has implemented a new daily driving charge on the ring road, which will last for a year.

The scatter graph below shows the number of vehicles per day, $N$, measured in tens of thousands, that use the ring road against the time, $t$, measured in months, from the date of the driving charge being introduced.

![Scatter graph showing a decline in daily vehicle numbers over 12 months after a driving charge was introduced.](assets/001-scatter-graph-showing-a-decline-in-daily-vehicle.png)

A simple model to relate $N$ and $t$ is given by the line of best fit:

$N=a+bt$

The line of best fit intersects the $N$-axis at the point $N=6$ and passes through the point $( 10 , 2 )$, as shown.

![Scatter graph showing vehicles per day declining over 12 months after a driving charge with a line of best fit that has a y-intercept of 6 and passes through the point (10, 2).](assets/005-scatter-graph-showing-vehicles-per-day-declining.png)

Use this information to find the values of $a$ and $b$.
parts.solution_md:
> *The line of best fit is given in the form of the equation of a straight line, *$y=mx+c$*, where *$m=b$* is the gradient, *$c=a$* is the *$y$*-intercept, *$x=t$* and *$y=N$

> *The *$y$*-intercept is the coordinate *$( 0 , 6 )$

$a=6$** ****[1]**

> *Use the coordinates *$( 0 , 6 )$* and *$( 10 , 2 )$* to find the gradient of the line of best fit*

$b=\frac{6-2}{0-10}=\frac{4}{-10}$

**[1]**

> *Simplify*

$b=-\frac{2}{5}$** ****[1]**

A simple model to relate N and t is given by the line of best fit: N = a + b t. The line of best fit intersects the N-axis at the point N = 6 and passes through the point (10, 2), as shown.

Use the model in part (a) to predict the total number of vehicles per day on the ring road 7 months after the driving charge was introduced.
parts.solution_md:
> *Substitute *$a=6$* and *$b=-\frac{2}{5}$* into the equation given for the line of best fit*

$N=6-\frac{2}{5}t$

> *Seven months after the ring road was introduced will be at the point when *$t=7$

> *Substitute *$t=7$* into the equation*

$N = 6 - \frac{2}{5} \times ( 7 )$

**[1]**

> *Use your calculator to find the answer*

$N=6-\frac{14}{5}=3.2$

> *Remember that the value of *$N$* is measured in tens of thousands, so multiply your answer by *$10000$

$3.2\times10000$

N equals a plus b t

Explain, with reason, whether or not the line of best fit should be continued beyond 12 months.
parts.solution_md:
> *It is given that the mayor is implementing the driving change for one year*
